subject: Kimberling et al. (1988)
object: Kimberling et al. (1988) described a 5-generation kindred descended from Sicilian immigrants with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease that was not linked to the alpha-hemoglobin complex on chromosome 16p. In linkage studies of 163 family members, 71 of whom were affected or at risk, the recombination frequency between the alpha-globin complex and the PKD1 region exceeded 24%, and the authors concluded that there is a second gene for ADPKD.

subject: Kimberling et al. (1988)
object: Kimberling et al. (1988) found that the clinical findings in the unlinked Sicilian-descended ADPKD kindred, in which diagnoses were confirmed by ultrasound, were indistinguishable from those in other families with polycystic kidney disease.

subject: Kimberling et al. (1988)
object: Kimberling et al. (1988) cautioned that, because of this locus heterogeneity, prenatal and presymptomatic diagnosis of ADPKD by linkage needs to be approached with caution until a method is found to tell the two forms apart.

subject: Romeo et al. (1988)
object: Romeo et al. (1988) found no linkage between autosomal dominant adult-type polycystic kidney disease and the alpha-globin genes on chromosome 16p in an Italian family. They concluded that the disorder can be caused by mutations in a second gene.

subject: Romeo et al. (1988)
object: Romeo et al. (1988) reported that the clinical features of polycystic kidney disease in the unlinked Italian family could not be told apart from those in families linked to chromosome 16.

subject: Romeo et al. (1988)
object: Romeo et al. (1988) pointed out that because there are two polycystic kidney disease genes, linkage must be shown separately in each family before DNA-probe predictive testing can be relied on.

subject: Nørby and Schwartz (1990)
object: Nørby and Schwartz (1990) proposed a possible locus for polycystic kidney disease on chromosome 2.

subject: Elles et al. (1990)
object: Elles et al. (1990) typed 24 families with adult-onset polycystic kidney disease for markers flanking the PKD1 locus on chromosome 16. The combined results gave a significant lod score in favor of linkage to PKD1.

subject: Elles et al. (1990)
object: Elles et al. (1990) found unusual features in 2 of 24 families: recombinations with markers flanking PKD1, including double recombinations, and, in one family, an unexpectedly high proportion of affected people. They considered whether the disease in these families might result from a mutation at a second locus, PKD2, not linked to PKD1. Using a test that compares the numbers of apparently nonrecombinant and doubly recombinant meioses, they concluded that neither their 2 families nor the published data on other families provided compelling evidence for a second locus.

subject: Elles et al. (1990)
object: Elles et al. (1990) suggested that, for genetic counseling in families too small to give their own evidence for or against linkage, the extra uncertainty could be handled by using a higher recombination rate.

subject: Kumar et al. (1990)
object: Kumar et al. (1990) genotyped members of a large ADPKD family not linked to chromosome 16 for 12 marker loci on both arms of chromosome 1. Multipoint analysis excluded the ADPKD2 locus from the region between D1S81 (pTHH33) and D1S67 (pHHH106) on the long arm and between Rh and PGM1 on the short arm. This excluded the disease locus from about 61% of chromosome 1, about 160 cM.

subject: Kumar et al. (1990)
object: Kumar et al. (1990) noted that autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease shows genetic heterogeneity: some families show linkage to markers on chromosome 16p and others do not. They studied a large family not linked to chromosome 16.

subject: Bachner et al. (1990)
object: Bachner et al. (1990) described a large 3-generation family with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Ultrasound screening of 60 family members found 20 individuals, aged 10 to 80 years, with one or several cysts in only one kidney and 7 individuals with cysts in both kidneys.

subject: Bachner et al. (1990)
object: In the family reported by Bachner et al. (1990), transmission of unilateral renal cysts appeared to be autosomal dominant, although some generations were skipped. The authors concluded that the family had a form of autosomal dominant PKD with reduced penetrance.

subject: Bachner et al. (1990)
object: Bachner et al. (1990) found no linkage between the disease and several markers of the PKD1 locus on 16p. Depending on the penetrance model and on how individuals with unilateral cysts were classified, lod scores for the 3-prime HVR marker ranged from 1.31 to -21.47 at theta = 0. Smith's test of heterogeneity gave a conditional probability of non-linkage between 0.9 and 1.0. The authors also considered other explanations: two distinct hereditary diseases in the family, or a new mutation in one branch together with a high frequency of isolated renal cysts.

subject: Kumar et al. (1991)
object: Kumar et al. (1991) studied a large Sicilian autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease kindred with over 250 members that was unlinked to the PKD1 locus on chromosome 16, supporting the existence of at least a second ADPKD locus.

subject: Kumar et al. (1991)
object: In the large Sicilian ADPKD kindred unlinked to chromosome 16, Kumar et al. (1991) analyzed 29 informative marker loci on 11 autosomes; linkage with the disease locus was significantly excluded for 17 marker loci, and there was no evidence of close linkage with the remaining loci.

subject: Ravine et al. (1992)
object: Ravine et al. (1992) compared 5 families (49 affected individuals) with ADPKD in which the PKD1 locus had been excluded against 18 PKD1-linked families (285 affected members). Compared with PKD1 patients, non-PKD1 patients lived longer (median survival 71.5 vs 56.0 years) and had a lower risk of progressing to renal failure (odds ratio 0.35). They were also less likely to have hypertension (adjusted odds ratio 0.29), were diagnosed at an older age (median 69.1 vs 44.8 years), and had fewer renal cysts at diagnosis.

subject: Ravine et al. (1992)
object: Ravine et al. (1992) concluded that ADPKD not linked to PKD1 on chromosome 16 has a much milder phenotype than PKD1-linked disease. No non-PKD1 family was ascertained through renal impairment clinics. Partly because of this milder severity, the authors suggested that the reported prevalence of the non-PKD1 genotype is probably an underestimate.

subject: Bear et al. (1992)
object: Bear et al. (1992) studied 17 Newfoundland families with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. In 10 families, ADPKD showed genetic linkage to markers for the PKD1 locus. In 2 families, ADPKD was not co-inherited with PKD1 markers.

subject: Bear et al. (1992)
object: Bear et al. (1992) found that in families whose ADPKD was not co-inherited with PKD1 markers, the mean age at onset of end-stage renal disease was 68.7 years (SE 1.7). In PKD1 families it was 56.3 years (SE 1.8; P = 0.01). In the 2 non-PKD1 families, only 11% of members younger than 30 years had kidney cysts.

subject: Bear et al. (1992)
object: Bear et al. (1992) estimated that in PKD1-linked families, ultrasonography gave false-negative diagnoses in 36% of members younger than 10 years and in 8% or less of older members. False-negative ultrasonographic diagnosis of PKD1 disease was unlikely after age 30 years. The risk of a false-negative result appeared largely restricted to families in which ESRD occurred relatively late.

subject: Jeffery et al. (1993)
object: Jeffery et al. (1993) reported a family of Sicilian origin with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease that was unlinked to chromosome 16 markers. LOD scores for the polymorphic markers 3-prime HVR and SM7, which flank the PKD1 locus, were -1.4 and -2.33, respectively, with theta max of 0.5 for each marker.

subject: Jeffery et al. (1993)
object: Jeffery et al. (1993) stated that the clinical phenotype of the Sicilian family was consistent with that of other ADPKD families not linked to 16p13.3, all reported from outside the United Kingdom. Those families showed milder progression than families linked to 16p13.3.

subject: Jeffery et al. (1993)
object: Jeffery et al. (1993) suggested that ADPKD may be much more genetically heterogeneous in the population than currently thought. Their reasoning was that clinic populations represent the most severe forms of the disease and that the non-PKD1 phenotype is less aggressive.

subject: Peters et al. (1993)
object: Peters et al. (1993) assigned a second gene for ADPKD to chromosome 4 using highly polymorphic microsatellite markers. In 8 families with clear evidence against linkage to chromosome 16 markers, linkage analysis with markers D4S231 and D4S423 gave a multipoint lod score of 22.42.

subject: Peters et al. (1993)
object: Peters et al. (1993) noted that ADPKD is genetically heterogeneous: a gene on the short arm of chromosome 16 accounts for roughly 86% of affected European families. They identified 8 families that showed clear evidence against linkage to chromosome 16 markers.

subject: Kimberling et al. (1993)
object: Kimberling et al. (1993) typed over 100 microsatellite markers spread across all chromosomes in informative members of the large Sicilian kindred in which genetic heterogeneity of ADPKD was first discovered. Renal ultrasonography confirmed whether each family member was affected or unaffected. The study localized a second ADPKD gene to chromosome 4q13-q23, flanked by markers D4S231 and D4S414, a segment of about 9 cM. The authors designated the new locus PKD4.

subject: Kimberling et al. (1993)
object: Kimberling et al. (1993) designated the second ADPKD locus, on chromosome 4q, as PKD4.

subject: Kimberling et al. (1993)
object: Kimberling et al. (1993) noted that at least two loci exist for ADPKD: one on 16p, and a second, less common locus that had not been mapped before this study. They stated that using flanking markers for both PKD1 and the new 4q locus would improve the accuracy of subtype diagnosis and of linkage-based presymptomatic diagnosis, by reducing errors caused by genetic heterogeneity.

subject: Fossdal et al. (1993)
object: Fossdal et al. (1993) used the polymorphic markers 3'HVR (D16S85), 16AC2.5 (D16S291) and SM7 (D16S283), which flank the PKD1 region on chromosome 16p13.3, to study linkage in 7 Icelandic families with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. In 4 families the disease locus was in the PKD1 region, and 3 families were unlinked to 16p13.3.

subject: Fossdal et al. (1993)
object: In one of the unlinked Icelandic ADPKD families, Fossdal et al. (1993) excluded the disease locus from part of the long arm of chromosome 2. They supported the theory that more than 2 loci are responsible for ADPKD. Their data also confirmed that the YNH24 locus (D2S44) maps to chromosome 2q13-q24.

subject: Coto et al. (1995)
object: Coto et al. (1995) studied 17 large Spanish families with ADPKD using ultrasonography and microsatellite markers closely linked to PKD1 on 16p13.3. Five of the 17 families showed negative linkage to 16p13.3, and in these families significant linkage to the PKD2 locus on 4q was obtained.

subject: Coto et al. (1995)
object: Coto et al. (1995) concluded that ADPKD in the Spanish population is genetically heterogeneous, but that mutations at only 2 loci, PKD1 and PKD2, are responsible for the disease in most if not all families; 12 of 17 families were linked to 16p13.3 and 5 to 4q.

subject: Coto et al. (1995)
object: Coto et al. (1995) found that renal cysts developed at an earlier age in PKD1 mutation carriers, and end-stage renal failure occurred at an older age in individuals with PKD2, indicating that ADPKD2 has a better prognosis than PKD1-linked disease.

subject: San Millán et al. (1995)
object: San Millán et al. (1995) confirmed linkage of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease to microsatellite markers on chromosome 4q in 8 Spanish families in which the disease was not linked to 16p13.3. A maximum lod score of 9.03 at a recombination fraction of 0.00 was obtained with marker D4S423. Multipoint linkage analysis and study of recombinant haplotypes placed the PKD2 locus between D4S1542 and D4S1563, defining a genetic interval of approximately 1 cM.

subject: San Millán et al. (1995)
object: San Millán et al. (1995) noted that ADPKD is genetically heterogeneous, with a gene defect at 16p13.3 responsible in approximately 86% of affected European families and a second locus at 4q13-q23 a candidate in the remaining families; their 8 Spanish families were unlinked to 16p13.3.

subject: Mochizuki et al. (1996)
object: Mochizuki et al. (1996) identified a second gene for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, PKD2, by positional cloning. They found nonsense mutations in PKD2 that segregated with the disease in 3 PKD2-linked families.

subject: Mochizuki et al. (1996)
object: Mochizuki et al. (1996) reported that the predicted 968-amino acid PKD2 protein has 6 transmembrane spans with intracellular N and C termini. It shares amino acid similarity with PKD1, with the C. elegans homolog of PKD1, and with the family of voltage-activated calcium (and sodium) channels, and it contains a potential calcium-binding domain.

subject: Veldhuisen et al. (1997)
object: Veldhuisen et al. (1997) screened the PKD2 gene by single-strand conformation polymorphism analysis in 35 families with the second type of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and identified 20 mutations. Most mutations seemed to be unique and occurred throughout the gene, with no evidence of clustering. Besides small deletions, insertions, and substitutions leading to premature translation stops, they found 1 amino acid substitution and 5 possible splice-site mutations.

subject: Veldhuisen et al. (1997)
object: Veldhuisen et al. (1997) suggested that the first step toward cyst formation in PKD2 patients is the loss of one functional copy of polycystin-2.

subject: Viribay et al. (1997)
object: Viribay et al. (1997) screened all 15 exons of the PKD2 gene in chromosome 4-linked ADPKD families using heteroduplex and SSCP analyses. They found 7 new mutations, a detection rate of about 90% in the population studied. Every mutation caused translation to stop early: 4 were nonsense changes and 3 were frameshifting deletions, one removing 4 T nucleotides and two each removing a single G nucleotide. All mutations were unique and were spread across the gene with no evidence of clustering.

subject: Viribay et al. (1997)
object: Viribay et al. (1997) compared the specific PKD2 mutations with the clinical profiles of the ADPKD2 families and found no clear correlation.

subject: Wu et al. (1998)
object: Wu et al. (1998) introduced a mutant exon 1 in tandem with the wild-type exon 1 at the mouse Pkd2 locus, creating an unstable allele that undergoes somatic inactivation by intragenic homologous recombination to produce a true null allele. Mice heterozygous and homozygous for this allele, as well as Pkd2 +/- mice, developed polycystic kidney and liver lesions that the authors described as indistinguishable from the human phenotype.

subject: Wu et al. (1998)
object: Wu et al. (1998) found that in all cases, renal cysts in Pkd2 mutant mice arose from renal tubular cells that had lost the ability to produce Pkd2 protein. They concluded that somatic loss of Pkd2 expression is both necessary and sufficient for renal cyst formation in ADPKD, suggesting that PKD2-related disease occurs by a cellular recessive mechanism.

subject: Pei et al. (1998)
object: Pei et al. (1998) screened 11 Canadian families with ADPKD for PKD2 mutations. Four families had previously documented linkage to PKD2. The other 7 were smaller families in which 1 or more affected members developed ESRD at age 70 or older. Using SSCP analysis of all 15 PKD2 exons in 1 affected member per family, they found mutations in 8 of 11 families (about 73%). The detection rate did not differ between the PKD2-linked families and the late-onset ESRD families.

subject: Pei et al. (1998)
object: Pei et al. (1998) found insertion or deletion of an adenosine in a polyadenosine tract ((A)8 at nucleotides 2152-2159) in exon 11 of PKD2 in 3 unrelated families. They suggested that this mononucleotide repeat tract is prone to mutation through slipped-strand mispairing.

subject: PKD2 insertion or deletion of an adenosine in (A)8 tract at nt 2152-2159, exon 11
object: PKD2

subject: Pei et al. (1998)
object: Pei et al. (1998) reported that all of the mutations lay between exons 1 and 11 and were predicted to produce a truncated polycystin-2 lacking the calcium-binding EF-hand domain and both cytoplasmic domains needed for interaction with polycystin-1 and with itself. They found no correlation between mutation location and disease severity, and suggested that most PKD2 mutations are inactivating.

subject: Pei et al. (1998)
object: Pei et al. (1998) noted that about 85% of ADPKD cases are caused by PKD1 mutations and that most of the rest are caused by PKD2 mutations. PKD1-linked families reach ESRD earlier than PKD2-linked families (mean age 56 vs 70 years).

subject: Hateboer et al. (1999)
object: Hateboer et al. (1999) compared clinical data from 291 individuals with PKD2 in 31 families with data from 333 individuals with PKD1 in 31 families and 398 geographically matched controls, in a European multicentre survey. The median age at death or onset of end-stage renal disease was 69.1 years in PKD2, compared with 53.0 years in PKD1 and 78.0 years in controls. The median age at presentation with kidney failure was 74.0 years in PKD2 and 54.3 years in PKD1.

subject: Hateboer et al. (1999)
object: Hateboer et al. (1999) found that PKD2 patients were less likely than PKD1 patients to have hypertension (odds ratio 0.25), a history of urinary tract infection (odds ratio 0.50), or hematuria (odds ratio 0.59). Women with PKD2 had a significantly longer median survival than men (71.0 vs 67.3 years), but no sex influence was apparent in PKD1. The authors concluded that although PKD2 is clinically milder than PKD1, it has a deleterious impact on overall life expectancy and cannot be regarded as a benign disorder.

subject: Torra et al. (1999)
object: Torra et al. (1999) studied 30 renal cysts from a patient with PKD2 whose germline mutation was a deletion covering most of the PKD2 gene. Loss of the wild-type allele (LOH) was found in 10% of cysts. SSCP screening of 6 exons found 8 different somatic mutations, all expected to produce truncated proteins. Overall, at least 37% of cysts had somatic mutations.

subject: PKD2 deletion that encompassed most of the disease gene
object: PKD2

subject: Torra et al. (1999)
object: Torra et al. (1999) found no LOH at the PKD1 gene or at locus D3S1478 in the cysts, which showed that the somatic changes were specific to PKD2. They suggested that second-hit inactivation of the normal PKD2 allele could be a crucial event in cyst formation in ADPKD type 2.

subject: Koptides et al. (1999)
object: Koptides et al. (1999) examined 21 renal cysts from both kidneys of one patient with ADPKD2 and found several novel somatic mutations in the PKD2 gene of the cyst epithelial cells. Seven of the 21 cysts (33%) carried the same C insertion in the inherited wild-type allele. In 2 other cysts, a nonsense mutation and a splice-site AG deletion were found in a PKD2 allele that could not be identified as either the inherited wild-type or the mutant allele. The authors suggested that ADPKD2, although dominantly inherited, arises through a cellular recessive mechanism, which supports a two-hit model of cyst formation.

subject: PKD2 C insertion within the inherited wild-type allele
object: PKD2

subject: PKD2 nonsense mutation
object: PKD2

subject: PKD2 splice site AG deletion
object: PKD2

subject: Wu et al. (2000)
object: Wu et al. (2000) produced two mutations in mouse Pkd2. One was an unstable allele (WS25) that can undergo somatic rearrangement by homologous recombination to form a null allele. The other was a true null allele (WS183). Pkd2 -/- mice died in utero between embryonic day 13.5 and birth. They had structural defects in cardiac septation and cysts in maturing nephrons and pancreatic ducts.

subject: Wu et al. (2000)
object: Wu et al. (2000) found that adult Pkd2 WS25/- mice developed kidney cysts, pancreatic ductal cysts, renal failure and early death. Median survival was 65 weeks, compared with 94 weeks in controls. The authors suggested that kidney, liver and pancreatic cysts form by a two-hit mechanism. Adult Pkd2 +/- mice had no cystic disease or renal failure, but their survival was between that of the other two groups. The authors took this as a first indication that Pkd2 haploinsufficiency harms long-term survival.

subject: Wu et al. (2000)
object: Based on their mouse models, Wu et al. (2000) concluded that kidney and liver cyst formation associated with Pkd2 deficiency occurs by a two-hit mechanism, in which a second somatic event inactivates the remaining Pkd2 allele.

subject: Koptides et al. (2000)
object: Koptides et al. (2000) studied DNA from individual cysts in the kidney of a patient with ADPKD1 who had a germline PKD1 mutation. They found somatic mutations in the PKD1 gene in some cysts and somatic mutations in the PKD2 gene in others. The cysts with a somatic PKD2 mutation were therefore trans-heterozygous, carrying mutations in both genes. The authors concluded that this was the first direct genetic evidence that polycystins 1 and 2 interact, perhaps as part of a larger complex.

subject: Koptides et al. (2000)
object: Koptides et al. (2000) referred to their own earlier study of a human ADPKD2 kidney, in which 9 of 23 cysts carried somatic mutations that inactivated the inherited normal PKD2 allele. They took this as support for a two-hit loss-of-function model of cyst formation in ADPKD2.

subject: Watnick et al. (2000)
object: Watnick et al. (2000) found somatic mutations of PKD2 in 71% of renal cysts analyzed from patients with ADPKD2, which supported a two-hit mechanism of cyst formation. In a subset of cysts that lacked PKD2 mutations, they found clonal somatic mutations of PKD1. Because the PKD1 and PKD2 products form heteromeric complexes, the authors suggested that trans-heterozygous mutations (a germline PKD2 mutation plus a somatic PKD1 mutation) may cause cysts.

subject: Pei et al. (2001)
object: Pei et al. (2001) studied a large ADPKD family (NFL10) previously excluded from linkage to both the PKD1 and PKD2 loci. Of 48 family members screened by ultrasonography and genotyped at both loci, 28 were affected with ADPKD, and haplotype inspection suggested bilineal disease from independently segregating PKD1 and PKD2 mutations.

subject: Pei et al. (2001)
object: In the NFL10 ADPKD family, Pei et al. (2001) used SSCP analysis to identify a PKD2 mutation, 2152delA (L736X), in 12 affected pedigree members.

subject: PKD2 c.2152dela / p.L736*
object: PKD2

subject: Pei et al. (2001)
object: Pei et al. (2001) found that when the PKD2 mutation carriers in family NFL10 were coded as unknown, linkage analysis with PKD1-locus markers gave significant lod scores (greater than 3.0), strongly supporting a PKD1 mutation in 15 other affected members who lacked the PKD2 mutation. This was the first documentation of bilineal disease in ADPKD, and the authors cautioned that bilineal disease must be considered as a confounder in the search for a PKD3 locus.

subject: Pei et al. (2001)
object: Pei et al. (2001) identified 2 affected individuals in family NFL10 who were trans-heterozygous for both the PKD1 and PKD2 mutations; they had more severe renal disease than individuals with either mutation alone. The authors concluded that trans-heterozygous PKD1/PKD2 mutations in humans are not necessarily embryonically lethal.

subject: Deltas (2001)
object: Deltas (2001) reviewed the mutations reported in the PKD2 gene. Mutations of all kinds were spread over the whole PKD2 sequence with no apparent significant clustering. Most families had their own private mutations, but a few recurrent mutations were reported in unrelated families.

subject: Deltas (2001)
object: Deltas (2001) noted that PKD1- and PKD2-related polycystic kidney disease have clinically indistinguishable courses. However, PKD2 mutation carriers had a milder course, with average onset 10 to 20 years later and a lower probability of reaching end-stage renal failure. The author also reported some evidence of genotype/phenotype correlation among PKD2 mutations.

subject: Deltas (2001)
object: Deltas (2001) suggested that renal cysts most probably arise after a second somatic event. This event would inactivate the inherited normal allele of the same gene, or possibly one allele of the other gene (PKD1 or PKD2), producing a trans-heterozygous state. Polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 were hypothesized to interact with each other and to take part in a common signaling pathway.

subject: Pennekamp et al. (2002)
object: Pennekamp et al. (2002) generated a knockout allele of Pkd2 in mouse. In addition to previously described malformations, homozygous mutant embryos showed right pulmonary isomerism and randomization of embryonic turning, heart looping, and abdominal situs.

subject: Pennekamp et al. (2002)
object: In homozygous Pkd2-null mouse embryos, Pennekamp et al. (2002) found that Leftb and nodal were not expressed in left lateral plate mesoderm, Ebaf was absent from floorplate, and Pitx2 was bilaterally expressed in posterior LPM but absent anteriorly. The embryonic midline was present with normal Foxa2 and shh expression, suggesting that polycystin-2 acts downstream or in parallel to shh and upstream of the nodal cascade.

subject: Pennekamp et al. (2002)
object: Pennekamp et al. (2002) found that mouse Pkd2 was ubiquitously expressed at headfold and early somite stages, with higher levels in floorplate and notochord.

subject: Bergmann et al. (2008)
object: Bergmann et al. (2008) reported perinatal deaths in a family with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and a PKD2 mutation.

subject: Bataille et al. (2011)
object: Bataille et al. (2011) reported 3 unrelated patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) who also had left-right laterality defects: one had dextrocardia and 2 had situs inversus totalis. No left-right anomalies were found in other members of the 3 families.

subject: Bataille et al. (2011)
object: In 3 unrelated probands with ADPKD and laterality defects, Bataille et al. (2011) screened PKD1 and PKD2 and found a pathogenic PKD2 mutation in each: a large gene deletion, a single-exon duplication, and an in-frame duplication. In each family, the mutation was present in all tested relatives with ADPKD and absent in unaffected relatives. The authors suggested a possible association between PKD2 mutations and heterotaxy. They based this on laterality defects in Pkd2-null mouse and zebrafish models and on finding PKD2 mutations in all 3 probands, even though PKD2 mutations account for only 15% of ADPKD families.

subject: PKD2 large gene deletion
object: PKD2

subject: PKD2 single-exon duplication
object: PKD2

subject: PKD2 in-frame duplication
object: PKD2

subject: Losekoot et al. (2012)
object: Losekoot et al. (2012) reported a patient with neonatal-onset polycystic kidney disease who was homozygous for an incompletely penetrant PKD2 missense variant. The homozygosity was caused by uniparental disomy.

subject: PKD2 incomplete penetrant PKD2 missense variant
object: PKD2

subject: Losekoot et al. (2012)
object: Losekoot et al. (2012) noted that ADPKD caused by a heterozygous mutation in PKD1 or PKD2 usually begins in adulthood, and that renal cystic disease is generally milder in PKD2 patients than in PKD1 patients.

subject: Khonsari et al. (2013)
object: Khonsari et al. (2013) found Pkd2 expression in craniofacial tissues. They studied mice with conditional deletion of Pkd2 in neural crest-derived cells, made using Wnt1Cre. The mutant mice had many signs of mechanical trauma, including fractured molar roots, distorted incisors, alveolar bone loss and compressed temporomandibular joints, as well as abnormal skull shapes. None of these phenotypes was seen at embryonic stages, when the head is under no significant mechanical stress in utero. The authors suggested that Pkd2 likely plays a critical role as a mechanoreceptor in craniofacial growth.

subject: Khonsari et al. (2013)
object: Facial anomalies had not previously been identified in ADPKD patients. Khonsari et al. (2013) took three-dimensional photographs of ADPKD patients' faces and analysed them using dense surface modelling. The analysis showed specific facial characteristics in the patients, some of which correlated with those of the Pkd2 conditional mutant mice.
